Pessimism of forecasts by cause of death

Source: R/derive-pessimism.R
mt_pessimism.Rd

Compares a forecast of all-cause mortality with the sum of separate forecasts of the causes of death, as Wilmoth (1995) does. Wilmoth calls the first the "total" forecast and the second the "all-cause" forecast; here they are "total" and "causes". The sum of cause forecasts tends to be higher, because it is dominated over time by the causes that fall slowest or rise. Every measure is computed path by path:

Usage

mt_pessimism(
  x,
  causes = NULL,
  var = "cause",
  total_level = "all",
  by = c("total", "age", "cause"),
  at = NULL,
  periods = NULL,
  h = 10,
  to = NULL,
  pairing = c("independent", "draw"),
  n_draws = 1,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
  paths = FALSE,
  seed = 1,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

An mt_draws object (forecast) or an mt_data object (observed deaths by cause, for the approximation from two periods).

causes

Optional mt_draws object with the forecasts of the causes (see Forecasts).

var

Stratum variable with the causes.

total_level

Level of var for all causes.

by

"total" (life expectancy), "age" (rates and m-ratios) or "cause" (contributions of the causes to the m-ratios).

at

Age at which life expectancy is computed (start of an age interval; default the first age).

periods

For data: a list of two vectors of observed years, the first and the second period (default: the two halves of the observed years).

h, to

For data: the number of forecast years after the last observed year, or the last forecast year.

pairing

"independent" or "draw": how the draws of x and causes are paired.

n_draws

For data: 1 (the observed deaths) or the number of Poisson draws.

probs

Quantile levels.

paths

Return the value of every path (columns draw and value) instead of the mean and quantiles.

seed

Seed of the shuffling of causes and of Poisson draws.

...

Passed to the life table (ax, open, k, omega, see life_table()) for life expectancy.

Value

A data.table with the stratum variables other than var, period, for by = "age" and "cause" also age_lo and age, for "cause" the column var with the cause, then measure, for "total" the age at, and the mean and quantiles over paths (q0.025, ...). With paths = TRUE, draw and value replace the mean and quantiles.

Details

  • by = "total": life expectancy at at of the total forecast (measure = "total") and of the sum of the causes ("causes"), and their "difference", total minus causes, the difference e0(Tot) - e0(All) that Wilmoth decomposes (Section 3, equation 15 and Table 5). It is positive where the forecast by cause is more pessimistic.

  • by = "age": the rates of the total forecast ("total") and of the sum of the causes ("causes"), and their ratio, the m-ratio of Wilmoth's equation (6), M(x, t) = sum_i m_i(x, t) / m(x, t) ("m_ratio"), his measure of the pessimism of forecasts by cause. It is above 1 where the forecast by cause is more pessimistic.

  • by = "cause": the contribution of each cause to the m-ratio minus 1 (equation 13), m_i(x, t) / m(x, t) - p_i(x), where p_i(x) is the proportion of the deaths at age x that are due to cause i in the last observed year (equation 5). The contributions of an age add up to its m-ratio minus 1 (Table 3).

Forecasts

For mt_draws, the forecast of all causes comes from x and the forecasts of the causes from causes. Without causes, x holds both: the strata of var at total_level and those of the causes, for example the forecasts of mt_fit() with a separate model for each stratum. With causes, for example the draws of a model of causes such as coda_causes(), x holds the total forecast: its strata at total_level, or all its strata if var is not a stratum variable of x. The causes are the levels of var other than total_level and the groups of a hierarchy stored in the object (see mt_aggregate_strata()), and the strata of the total and of the causes are matched on the other stratum variables (for example sex and deprivation quintile). The causes should cover all deaths: a warning reports observed causes that do not add up to the observed total in the last training year.

Wilmoth derives equations (6) and (13) for proportional rate of change models, which project the observed rates of the last year t0 with constant annual factors. Equation (6) is defined for any forecast; for other models, and for models whose forecasts start from fitted rates (his footnote 2), the m-ratio is still the ratio of the forecasts and the contributions still add up to the m-ratio minus 1, but the m-ratio of the first forecast years also contains the jump-off of the models (see mt_jump_off()).

Draws of two objects come from different models and are independent: by default (pairing = "independent") the draws of causes are shuffled before they are paired with those of x, as in mt_decompose(). Use pairing = "draw" when causes is derived from the draws of x.

Approximation from two periods

For an mt_data object, mt_pessimism() computes Wilmoth's approximation from the distributions of deaths by cause in two periods (Section 3, equations 12 and 14). The rates of each cause and period are its deaths divided by the exposures, both summed over the years of the period (Appendix C), and the total rate is the sum of the causes (a warning reports causes that do not add up to the level total_level of the data, where it exists). Both are projected from the midpoint t2 of the second period at the geometric mean rate of change between the midpoints t1 and t2, the "first-to-last" method of his equations (8) to (11) applied to periods: m(x, t) = m2(x) (m2(x) / m1(x))^((t - t2) / (t2 - t1)). The m-ratio of these forecasts is equation (12), sum_i p_i (p_i / q_i)^((t - t2) / (t2 - t1)), with q_i and p_i the proportions of deaths by cause in the first and the second period, and the contributions are equation (14). Wilmoth shows (Appendix B) that this m-ratio exceeds 1 at every horizon unless the two distributions are equal. The difference of life expectancies is the quantity that his Table 5 decomposes by age and cause.

The default periods are the first and the second half of the observed years, the "first-to-second" method that Wilmoth uses for his decompositions; with an odd number of years the middle year is left out, so that the halves have the same length (package-specific, reference unknown). His "first-to-last" method uses the first and the last three years, for example periods = list(1951:1953, 1988:1990). The forecast years are those after the last observed year (h, to).

With n_draws = 1 (default) the observed deaths are used. With more draws the deaths are Poisson draws, as in mt_observed(), and the intervals show the sampling variation of the approximation (package-specific, reference unknown). A cause without deaths at an age in both periods contributes nothing there (the dashes of Wilmoth's Table 3). A cause without deaths in the first period and with deaths in the second would grow without bound: its deaths in the first period are set to 0.5, as rwd() does with zero counts, with a warning (package-specific, reference unknown).

References

Wilmoth JR (1995). Are mortality projections always more pessimistic when disaggregated by cause of death? Mathematical Population Studies 5(4): 293-319. doi:10.1080/08898489509525409

See also

mt_coherence() for the ratio of summed strata to aggregates in any hierarchy, mt_decompose() for decompositions of life expectancy by age and cause, reconciled() and coda_causes() for forecasts by cause that add up.

Examples

x <- mt_example_causes(years = 2000:2019)
# separate Lee-Carter models for all causes and for each cause
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
mt_pessimism(fc, at = 65)[period == 2029]
#>       sex period    measure    at       mean     q0.025       q0.5     q0.975
#>    <char>  <num>     <char> <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>
#> 1: female   2029      total    65 23.7035780 23.3216321 23.7116535 24.0669705
#> 2: female   2029     causes    65 23.4944717 23.2815900 23.5195917 23.6932909
#> 3: female   2029 difference    65  0.2091063 -0.2813627  0.2067860  0.6321682
#> 4:   male   2029      total    65 19.5776676 19.1667844 19.6262465 19.9755737
#> 5:   male   2029     causes    65 19.4764975 19.3181567 19.4929899 19.6335253
#> 6:   male   2029 difference    65  0.1011701 -0.3036909  0.1087295  0.6226814
m <- mt_pessimism(fc, by = "age")
m[measure == "m_ratio" & period == 2029 & age %in% c("50", "70", "90")]
#>       sex period age_lo    age measure     mean    q0.025     q0.5   q0.975
#>    <char>  <num>  <num> <char>  <char>    <num>     <num>    <num>    <num>
#> 1: female   2029     50     50 m_ratio 1.009184 0.9269285 1.005622 1.102265
#> 2: female   2029     70     70 m_ratio 1.019328 0.9395110 1.016333 1.115691
#> 3: female   2029     90     90 m_ratio 1.028305 0.9614267 1.028123 1.085640
#> 4:   male   2029     50     50 m_ratio 1.026957 0.9366452 1.035116 1.099733
#> 5:   male   2029     70     70 m_ratio 1.017059 0.9580756 1.016272 1.096000
#> 6:   male   2029     90     90 m_ratio 1.010961 0.9581379 1.011347 1.074437
# Wilmoth's approximation from the halves 2000-2009 and 2010-2019
a <- mt_pessimism(x, by = "cause", to = 2039)
a[period == 2039 & age == "70"]
#>       sex period age_lo    age  cause      measure        mean      q0.025
#>    <char>  <num>  <num> <char> <char>       <char>       <num>       <num>
#> 1: female   2039     70     70    cvd contribution -0.10070629 -0.10070629
#> 2: female   2039     70     70 cancer contribution  0.12682346  0.12682346
#> 3: female   2039     70     70  other contribution  0.04443719  0.04443719
#> 4:   male   2039     70     70    cvd contribution -0.10560148 -0.10560148

#>           q0.5      q0.975
